note: git grep -E with a backslash-b word boundary returns NOTHING and exits 1 — POSIX ERE has no backslash-b, so the search is silently empty and reads exactly like: no citations to fix. During The Underworld decision renumber, git grep -E ...0142... found 0 files while git grep -l 0142 found 36. Use git grep -P for backslash-b, backslash-d, lookarounds. It was caught ONLY by running the same pattern against a number known to be present and watching that control come back empty too. Positive-control any grep whose emptiness you are about to trust. Second half of the same trap: a bare-number sweep hits numeric data (-0.0142 in tables, four-digit runs in census CSVs and geojson), so scope to prose and eyeball every hit.
